content.title: 250,000 miles from Earth? Mind-boggling facts about Artemis II.
content.text: Launching from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida during a full moon on April Fool's Day, the Artemis II mission is scheduled to be humanity's first voyage toward the moon in over 50 years.The second mission under NASA's multibillion-dollar moon program, it will send three Americans and one Canadian on a 10-day journey around the moon and back.The Artemis II crew is set to become the first humans in over 50 years — since Apollo 17 in December 1972 — to travel beyond low Earth orbit, loop around the moon, and see its far side, Aerotime said. While no landing is in store for the astronauts, the mission serves as a vital test flight to lay the groundwork for humans to make it back to the surface in as little as two years.During the journey, the crew is set to experience forces that boggle the mind:Once the engines — alongside the two solid rocket boosters — get SLS off the pad, the rocket goes soaring off into space at approximately 17,000 mph. At that speed, you could get from Los Angeles to New York in about 10 minutes. It's the equivalent to 22 times the speed of sound.Standing as tall as the Statue of Liberty, the rocket they will be launched in is one of the largest and most powerful ever built. The Artemis II Space Launch System (SLS) rocket and Orion capsule, when fully stacked, stand 322 feet tall. This makes it taller than the Statue of Liberty (but shorter than the Apollo-era Saturn V.)At its farthest, Artemis II will be about 250,000 miles from Earth. If they launch as scheduled, NASA expects that on April 6, they will surpass Apollo 13's record when it reached 248,655 miles from Earth.Visual explainer: See how Artemis mission will get to the moon, step-by-stepHere are the mission basics by the numbers:4 astronauts: Reid Wiseman • Victor Glover • Christina Koch • Jeremy Hansen10 days: Mission length685,000 miles: Total journey around the moon and back4,700 miles: Furthest distance beyond the moon’s far side322 feet: Height of NASA’s Space Launch System rocket8.8 million pounds: Thrust at liftoff — the most powerful operational rocket25,000 mph: Speed during Earth reentryFirsts: First crewed lunar flight in 50+ years; First woman, first Black astronaut, first Canadian beyond low Earth orbitThe full moon rises as Artemis II sits on Pad 39B at Kennedy Space Center Feb. 1, 2026.Fascinating facts about Artemis II:Artemis 1, which was uncrewed, flew 80 miles above the surface, for context. Apollo missions flew less than 70 miles from the surface. The lunar reconnaissance orbiter flies by at about 31 miles high.The Artemis II crew will travel between 4,600 and 6,000 miles above the surface of the moon. The distance is variable because exactly how close the Artemis II crew will fly to the moon will depend on when they launch, as the moon will be in a different spot for each of the possible launch dates.Space Launch System: 322 feet tall is shorter than the 363-feet tall Saturn V used for the Apollo missions but about 17% more powerful, launching atop 8.8 million pound of thrust. It's the most powerful rocket NASA has ever launched.Orion capsule is 11 feet high and 16 1/2 feet wideLaunch site: Launch Complex 39B is far from being as prolific or historic as 39A at the Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida. Since construction ended in 1968, Launch Complex 39B has supported 60 launches as of January 2025. However, it is the site of one Saturn V launch on the Apollo 10 mission in 1969.How tall is the Artemis II SLS?More graphics: See how Artemis launch returns humans to the moon after five-decade absence(This story was updated to meet our standards.)This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Artemis II by the numbers. How fast, far will the crew go?
